books.section: America Transformed into the Industrial Giant of the World (1870–1910)
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Emory R. Johnson, American Railway Transportation (1908), Interstate Commerce Commission railroad mileage; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), Table IX, steel output

stimulus.text:
The table shows two measures of American industrial growth, 1870-1900.

| Year | Miles of railroad in operation | Steel produced (millions of tons) |
| 1870 | 52,922 | 0.07 |
| 1880 | 93,296 | 1.25 |
| 1890 | 163,597 | 4.28 |
| 1900 | 193,346 | 10.19 |
stimulus.source_note: Railroad mileage from Emory R. Johnson, American Railway Transportation (1908), using Interstate Commerce Commission figures; steel output from the Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), Table IX. The lesson script gives the same scale in round numbers: about 35,000 miles of track in 1865 and over 190,000 by 1900.

stem: The table best supports which conclusion about the relationship between railroads and steel?

options.text: Steel mills caused railroad building to stop after 1890
options.misconception: Railroad mileage kept growing after 1890, from about 167,000 to about 193,000 miles.

options.text: Railroads replaced steel as the leading industry
options.misconception: The table shows both growing, not one replacing the other.

options.text: Steel output grew only after railroad building ended
options.misconception: Both grew in the same decades, so steel did not wait for railroads to end.

options.text: The two grew together, since each needed the other

rationales.A: Railroad mileage still rose after 1890, so steel did not stop it.
rationales.B: Both industries grew side by side, so neither replaced the other.
rationales.C: Steel output rose while railroad mileage was also rising.
rationales.D: The two series rise in step, and each industry fed the other.
rationales.general:
Ask what the two columns do together.
1. Railroad mileage rises from about 53,000 miles in 1870 to about 193,000 in 1900.
2. Steel output rises from 0.07 to 10.19 million tons over the same years.
3. Neither series waits for the other to finish; they climb in the same decades.
4. Background from the books: cheap steel made rails affordable, and railroads carried ore, coal, and finished steel.
Remember: when two industries rise in step, look for how each fed the other.
